https://t.co/23R3OuxRVz

2061693014787993951.text:
3/4
In an economy in which unit labor costs are among the lowest in the world, you would expect the most competitive producers to specialize in labor-intensive industries, but in China many of them are rushing into politically-preferred industries because in these industries...

2061693017644261673.text:
4/4
the cost of capital (including subsidized equipment and logistics) is even lower. They get unlimited credit at low rates and with no hard-budget constraints.

Under these conditions, it is natural to shift even more from labor-intensive industries to capital-intensive ones.

2061666911868289059.text:
1/6
Financial Times: "A company-level OECD analysis of government subsidies across 15 key industrial sectors found that nearly 60 per cent of Chinese firms’ global market share gains since 2005 could be attributed to subsidies."
https://t.co/o2mcZeaagi

2061666922358288749.text:
5/6
The OECD study notes that firms that are more efficient and productive (i.e. that create greater value in their production processes) are nonetheless unable to compete with firms that receive subsidies that are high enough to make them globally competitive.

2061666924824526983.text:
6/6
The short term implication is that global resources shift not to their most productive users but rather to their most subsidized users. The longer term implication is that this process can go on only as long as the subsidies can be funded.

2061446666121523446.text:
1/5

2061446676234047833.text:
4/5
By the way the fact that the US is running huge current account deficits in spite of running some of the highest levels of income inequality in its history (income inequality should force up the saving rate just as much as "fiscal discipline" would) suggests that it...

2061446680805777797.text:
5/5
is not low American saving that drives the US trade deficit, but rather large, persistent US trade deficits (driven mainly by the need of surplus countries to exchange their surpluses for claims on US assets) that drive down US saving.
https://t.co/Pw1X70DuT1

2061393764136914975.text:
1/3
It is pretty meaningless to say that China "has a comparative advantage in industrial policy itself". 

It is certainly true that Chinese industrial policy is reinforced by aggressive intervention in its external accounts.
https://t.co/60hWZFoPpD

2061393766745829730.text:
2/3
But this just means (as we've known for decades) that successful mercantilist policies externalize the cost of a country's domestic industrial policies.

This is not a comparative advantage. It is a way of securing competitive advantage.
https://t.co/NLoqJyVwKe

2061393769291735540.text:
3/3
As long as trade partners don't retaliate by intervening in their own external accounts, this competitive advantage can be sustained. But once they do, it quickly disappears, which is not what happens when a country truly has a comparative advantage in production.
